statement: If clients send a heartbeat every 10 seconds, each sends 6 heartbeats per minute; with 1 million active users (active, not total users) the system receives 6 million requests per minute.
detail: The teacher frames this as the more interesting challenge after storage: 'now things are becoming scary'.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If there are 1 million active users, not total users, active users, then your system will get 6 million requests per minute.

statement: Every heartbeat results in one database call (an update), so a single database has to absorb about 6 million updates per minute, and with that many writes the database would start to choke.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Your database having to do so many writes, 6 million updates per minute, your database would start to choke.
flags: check: "206 million" - possibly "to do 6 million"; 6 million said before and after

statement: The online/offline store is a classic case where storage is not the problem but computation is: the whole dataset fits in 8 GB (8 GB for 1 million entries is peanuts for a database), while supporting 6 million requests per minute is the challenge.
detail: The concern is the number of queries fired, each doing an update on the database.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now here is a classic case where storage is not a problem. Computation is.

statement: Sharding and partitioning, the other ways to handle this load, are discussed in coming weeks; this part focuses on connection pooling instead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we'll talk about sharding partitioning in coming weeks.

statement: Connection pooling is an optimization that very few people talk about, and one everyone should know about for a write-heavy load like this.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One thing that I want to bring out is something that very few people talk about is connection pooling.

statement: Each heartbeat is an HTTP POST request over a TCP connection; when it arrives, the API server creates a second TCP connection with the database to write the update.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When the request comes in, API server creates a connection with the database and writes something. So this is another TCP connection.

statement: Setting up a TCP connection requires the three-way handshake and terminating it a two-way teardown, so a fresh connection costs five network trips for every single call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So five network trips for every single call.

statement: The single line drawn between the API server and the database on a design diagram, usually drawn without a thought, stands for an expensive connection-establishment process.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the one line that we draw like this on the diagram, like this, without giving a thought, is an expensive process.

statement: Each heartbeat write is a micro update: a pointed update of one row indexed by primary key, so the database does the bare minimum and most of the time goes into establishing the TCP connection, the biggest performance bottleneck here.
detail: Connection pooling is added to make this better and to put less load on the database.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Most of the time that is being spent here is in establishing this TCP connection, which is an expensive process.

statement: Connection pooling: instead of shutting each TCP connection down, keep a bunch of connections open between the server and the database and reuse them, because with micro updates much of the time is wasted establishing and tearing down connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Who asked the TCP connection to shut down? Don't shut it down. Let the TCP connection be open between your server and your database.

statement: Example: on startup the API server creates three TCP connections with the database and keeps them handy on the side; whenever it needs to fire any query (select, update, insert), it uses one of them that no one else is using.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: My API server creates three TCP connections with my database on startup.

statement: When a request comes in, the server picks one available connection from the pool and marks it unavailable; since it is already established, it only fires the query and gets the response - one request and one response - saving the five network trips of setup and teardown.
detail: The teacher says he will also talk about the implementation of picking and marking connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It does not have to reestablish the TCP connections and terminate it. So it saves five network trips

statement: Connection pooling has two benefits: it makes the API call very fast, and it reduces the load on the database even though the number of queries stays the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This way you make your API call very fast, number one. Number two, you reduce the load on the database.

statement: Establishing a TCP connection is expensive for the database itself: it must read the handshake packets (first packet in, acknowledgement out, third packet in), spending CPU to process them, network bandwidth to read them, and OS buffers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Establishing the TCP connection is an expensive process for your database.

statement: By pre-establishing connections and reusing them, the database saves mainly CPU and network work (the teacher first said memory too, then corrected to 'not really memory'), which dramatically reduces its load given the updates are one-row micro updates.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are saving the CPU and network, that additional work that CPU network would have to do

statement: Adding a connection pool gives a performance boost in client-side response time, reduces load on the database (freeing it to fire other queries), saves infrastructure cost and makes the database much more performant.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It will save your infrastructure cost.

statement: When you define a connection pool you define a minimum and a maximum number of connections (e.g. a minimum of three to start with).
detail: Raised as the question 'how many connections should you create?'. With three connections and three concurrent requests each picks one; a fourth concurrent request finds no available connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you define a connection pool, you define what is the minimum number of connections? What is the maximum number of connections?

statement: Databases such as MySQL, Postgres and Redis all support connection pooling, and there are libraries that manage the pool for you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, database, MySQL, Postgres, Redis, everyone supports connection pooling. And there are libraries who manage it for you.

statement: When all pooled connections are busy (e.g. a fourth concurrent request with three connections), the first option is to wait until one of the running queries releases its connection and then use it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Fourth concurrent request came in. It does not have a connection to make a call to the database.

statement: The second option, if the request does not want to wait, is to establish a new TCP connection, fire the query and add that connection to the pool, so the pool grows from three to four - stretching the connection pool on demand.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is stretching the connection pool on demand.

statement: Stretching without a limit is a problem: with millions of requests each creating its own connection and adding it to the pool, so you don't do that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if let's say there are millions of requests coming in, everyone creates their own connections and adds to the connection pool, then that's a problem.

statement: Configure a maximum on the pool, e.g. minimum 3 and maximum 100: each server then cannot create more than 100 connections to the database, and a 101st concurrent request waits for one of the 100 to be released.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: hey, minimum three, maximum 100. So each server cannot create more than 100 connections to the database

statement: Every database has a limit on the number of TCP connections it can hold, so a problem creeps in when hundreds of servers each create 100 connections to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every database has a limit on the number of TCP connections that it can hold

statement: The connection pool is responsible for terminating unused connections: you configure a TTL per connection (e.g. terminate a connection not used for 10 minutes), which reduces the number of connections a server holds on the database.
detail: Example: if one API server created four connections and one is unused for 10 minutes, the pool deletes it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you can also configure a time that says that this is the TTL of my connection.

statement: A connection pool is not a separate process or service: it is a simple library running inside the API server that creates the pool of database connections.
detail: The teacher remarks that nowadays, for some reason, everyone thinks everything is a service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Connection pool is a simple library that is running in the API server of yours, which is creating this pool of connections to the database.

statement: Implementation: when the server boots it creates multiple database connection objects and puts them in a blocking queue; a caller pops a connection if one is there, otherwise it waits (a loop) until someone puts one back.
detail: There are a ton of connection pool implementations on GitHub, but the idea remains the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You put them in a blocking queue and you read them as you need it.

statement: The pool gives a massive performance boost here because each update is a tiny one-row update by primary key (it goes straight to that B+ tree node and updates it), so spending an expensive connection setup on it would be wasteful.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: literally goes to that B plus tree node and updates it, right? Dead simple system.

statement: For a big SQL query, the time to run the query is long enough to outweigh the benefit of a connection pool; the pool's big gain comes when the updates are micro.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it was a big SQL query, then the time to run that query is long enough for you to outweigh the benefits...

statement: Whenever you fire a bunch of micro updates on a database - and in general - having a connection pool is always a great option; if your existing codebase has none, check whether adding one gives you a big performance gain.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: having a connection pool and in general, having a connection pool is always a great option.

statement: The online/offline design can be copied almost as-is to build failure detection in a distributed system: all nodes send heartbeats to a central server that tracks which are alive, and a node whose heartbeat stops arriving is down.
detail: Example: building your own AWS with a bunch of EC2 machines, you need to know when a machine is down. There are some protocol differences here and there.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In a distributed system, all the nodes send a heartbeat to a central server that keeps track which one is alive...

statement: Example: when building your own load balancer, the same heartbeat system detects that a backend machine is down so you stop forwarding requests to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say we are building our own load balancer

statement: Observe the pattern and the core properties a system needs rather than memorising the question and its answer, and build intuition for building systems from them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So observe the pattern, observe the core properties that we need and then build an intuition around building systems, right?

statement: If newly spun-up API servers need connections beyond the database's TCP connection limit (e.g. during a special event), the new server cannot create one; it waits, retrying in a loop, and succeeds only when an existing server terminates a connection.
detail: Question from a student (Student 4) about the time frame when scaling API servers pushes connections past the limit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It will keep on trying to establish the connection forever.
flags: check: possibly the start of the teacher's answer

statement: The fix is to scale up the database to handle more TCP connections: the size of the database depends on the number of concurrent queries, because the concurrency you want to support determines the concurrent connections it must handle.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the concurrency that you would want to support in a system would determine the number of concurrent connections that your database would need to handle.

statement: In most cases the most common bottleneck of a database is the maximum number of connections it can handle, so you need to know that number.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the most common bottleneck of a database is the maximum number of connections that it can handle.

statement: To support more concurrency than the database's connection limit, scale it vertically; otherwise go for sharding - the two common ways, discussed next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And if you want to support concurrency more than that, you vertically scale your system. Otherwise, you go for sharding.

statement: Asked whether managed DynamoDB gives better value than a self-managed Redis that must be autoscaled on the fly: with a startup or small, lean team that lacks the ability to manage it, go for DynamoDB or another managed solution.
detail: Question from a student (Student 4).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You go for DynamoDB or any managed solution when you have a lean team.

statement: Self-hosting Redis requires a team with expertise to manage it; without that, use a managed Redis (Redis Labs, AWS, GCP all offer a variant); self-host only with the expertise and engineering bandwidth - otherwise throw money at cloud providers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You throw money at cloud providers and get things done.

statement: If pooled connections expire through their TTL (e.g. 50 of 100 expired) and more requests arrive, the pool creates new connections up to its maximum: with a maximum of 100 and 50 open, a 51st concurrent request establishes a new connection and adds it to the pool.
detail: Question from a student (Student 2). The 01:22:34 line adds that the new connection is added with the same expiration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But now you only 50 but 51st request came in, so it would establish a new connection and put it in the connection pool.
flags: check: speaker of the 01:22:34 line ("Teacher?") - says the new connection gets the same expiration

statement: The pool does not always hold 100 connections: 100 is the maximum, and the actual number depends on the number of requests coming in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, at max there will be 100.

statement: Asked whether the number of connections, rather than the data, decides how to scale the database here (a 'brilliant question'): yes, because updates are very small and the access pattern is key-value.
detail: Question from a student (Amrita).
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why number of connections is an important factor? Because updates are very small, right? It's a key-value kind of access pattern.

statement: With micro reads and micro writes (update one row; reads like 'given a user, give me the row'; no massive analytics queries), reads and writes are fast and the bottleneck becomes the network - specifically establishing TCP connections.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And in network, establishing the TCP connection becomes a bottleneck.

statement: If queries are massive aggregations joining 10 or 15 tables, where executing a query takes longer than establishing a connection, don't stress connections; focus on the CPU and memory side of the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then you would not stress more on this. You'd focus more on the CPU side and the memory side of the database.

statement: The maximum number of TCP connections a server can handle (a database is a process running on a server) depends on its RAM and on the network card of the instance.
detail: Question from a student (DK): is the concurrent-connection limit documented or must it be benchmarked?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Maximum number of connections that a server can handle depends on the RAM that it holds, depends on the network card on that instance.

statement: On a managed service such as AWS RDS, the provider gives a formula you can run to see the connection limit and shows it in the UI; managed-service documentation lists how many concurrent connections each database size handles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: On AWS, if you're using RDS or any database, it gives you a formula that you can fire and see the number.

statement: For a self-managed database, benchmark: pick a machine with high network capacity and measure how many concurrent connections it holds; the number also depends on the kind of load (a very high sustained load may not be met), so it is always better to benchmark.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you are doing self-managed, then do a benchmark.

statement: In most cases you need an instance with a dedicated attached network card (maybe several); every cloud provider has a special class of high-network-bandwidth instances for supporting large numbers of TCP connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every cloud provider has this special class of instances that offers you high network bandwidth for you to support large number of TCP connections.

statement: A student proposed that there are two parameters for deciding whether to scale a database vertically or horizontally: concurrent connections and the size of the database.
detail: The teacher broadened it rather than rejecting it: scaling is decided by four things - memory, CPU, disk and network.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So overall there are two parameters to scale the DB. Concurrent connection and one is the size of the DB
flags: check: likely DK's follow-up; split point inside the 01:27:14 segment

statement: There are only four things in computer science - memory, CPU, disk and network (no fifth; GPU counted under CPU) - and these four determine scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There are only four things in computer science. Only four: memory, CPU, disk and network. There is no fifth.

statement: CPU-intensive use cases: doing massive aggregations on your data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you are doing massive aggregations on your data, that's CPU intensive.

statement: Memory-intensive use cases: pulling in a lot of data to process, such as massive joins.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is memory intensive, where you're pulling in a lot of data that you would want to process, like massive joins that you are doing.

statement: Disk-bound use cases: storing large amounts of data on disk until disk becomes the bottleneck; data warehouses fall in this category.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then disk, where you're storing large amount of data on the disk

statement: Network-bound use cases: the number of queries you can fire on a server (here, the database) is limited by the network capacity of that machine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your amount of queries that you would want to fire on a server is limited by the network capacity of that machine

statement: Scaling, horizontal or vertical, is defined on these four parameters; vertical scaling has a limit, so a good distributed system should be made horizontally scalable, which is where sharding comes up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if you're building a good distributed system, make it horizontally scalable, which is where sharding comes up.

statement: Asked how to build intuition for when to use connection pooling, the answer given is: always use it.
detail: Question from a student (Student 7), whose follow-up asks how to choose the pool minimum and maximum.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: So you're saying always, always use, right?
flags: check: "always, always use" may be the teacher interjecting

statement: The pool minimum is typically 3 or 5, because when the pool is exhausted connections can be created on the fly anyway.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Okay, so minimum typically people start with three or five, right?

statement: Pool maximum per server = maximum connections the database supports / maximum number of servers you will have at any time; e.g. a database handling 1000 connections with at most 100 servers gives 10 per server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You need to know the maximum number of connections that your database can support divided by the maximum number of servers that you would have...

statement: Set the maximum somewhat above the average (e.g. 15 instead of 10) because one server may get more requests than others, and if the database cannot establish a connection the server waits anyway; maximum is typically 1.2x the average - a practice the teacher has seen, not a standard.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So maximum is typically 1.2x of the average.

statement: Have the right telemetry on the connection pool - how it performs, the number of connections in the pool at any moment, the number of servers; a week of production gives the numbers to tune it better.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you give your production system one week, you will have those numbers on which you would be able to tune it better.

statement: The best way to tune a connection pool is to start with a conservative mindset, observe the metrics and then retune.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the best way to tune it is start with a conservative mindset, observe the metrics and then retune it.

statement: For a festival where online users jump (e.g. 2x) and updates arrive faster than the database can apply them, a student proposed vertically scaling the systems; the teacher agreed: 'Always.'
detail: Proposal from a student (Rahul). The student felt connection pooling 'messes things up' when update time exceeds the incoming rate.
case_study: Online/offline indicator: every active user sends a heartbeat that updates one row in the database.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can increase, vertically scale the systems that we have.

statement: Vertically scaling for a spike is fine because you scale up and bring it back down; there is no way out - the database must support the concurrent requests you aim for: for 2x, first make sure it supports it, then tune the pool.
detail: Answer to the student's worry that scaling up just for a festival is not feasible.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You scale it up and you basically bring it down, right?

statement: A much better answer to traffic spikes comes later in the course, when flash sales are discussed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When we discuss flash sale, you will have a very good answer for this.

statement: For a spike: vertically scale the database to handle the concurrent requests you need, then tune the connection pool maximum (maybe not the minimum), since vertically scaled servers can also handle more requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you may have to tune your connection pool maximum, may not be minimum, but the maximum size of a connection pool

statement: Knowing the tech unit economics is very important in the real world; have the right monitoring tools to make these decisions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Knowing the tech unit economic is very important when you are operating in real world.

statement: Each session has one 5-7 minute break; after this break come about 20-25 minutes on databases and 20-25 minutes on caching, and the other four foundational topics are covered later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database and caching is what we'll cover today and other four we'll cover at the end.

statement: The teacher originally started the session with the foundational topics but it became too theoretical, so he switched to the online/offline indicator first to get into the groove.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I started from here, it become too theoretical, like, now scrap this, let me start with online offline

statement: Six core components to think about when designing most (not all) systems: database, caching, scaling, delegation, concurrency, communication; any system discussed, including the online/offline indicator, shows all six as key design decisions.
detail: Two (database, caching) are covered today, the other four tomorrow.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database, caching, scaling, delegation, concurrency, communication.

statement: Caching gets only 5-7 minutes today, but many caching use cases and how to improve them come up over the course; day one keeps things simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Caching, five minutes, seven minutes thing

statement: Databases are taught through designing a simple multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user can post multiple blogs and there are multiple users; no fancy recommendations.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So one user can post multiple blogs and there are multiple users in the system.

statement: The users table has id (auto-increment), name (what is rendered) and bio (a small text, around 128 characters).
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So users will have ID, name and bio.

statement: The blogs table has id, author_id (who wrote it), title, body, published_at (when it was published) and is_deleted.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In blogs you have ID, author ID.

statement: Soft delete: an is_deleted column; when the user deletes a row you just mark is_deleted as true instead of removing it.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: is deleted as a soft delete column, where if user deletes it, you just mark is deleted as true.

statement: Many tables, including in your own organization, have an is_deleted column; soft deletes are extremely important, including for the performance of the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now soft deletes are extremely important to ensure the performance of your database.

statement: Hard delete: firing a DELETE query on the database; the data cannot be recovered afterwards.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you just fire a delete query on your database, it's a hard delete. It means you cannot recover that corresponding data again.

statement: Reason 1 for soft delete - recoverability: if you want to let a user recover something they deleted (e.g. a deleted blog), use soft delete.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So when you need recoverability, you use soft.

statement: Google Drive is soft delete: a deleted file goes into the trash, stays there for 30 days, and can be recovered from the trash during that time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In Google Drive you delete a file, it goes into trash, and for 30 days it stays in the trash

statement: Reason 2 for soft delete - archival: content a user put effort into is rich data (e.g. to train machine-learning models, 'build another ChatGPT'); hard deleting it loses it.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If user marks it as delete and you hard deleted, that rich data is gone.

statement: For archival: when the user deletes, soft delete the row and run a job that pulls out soft-deleted rows and puts them into S3 or another blob storage for machine-learning training and other uses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: run a job that pulls out this soft deleted rows and puts into S3 or any blob storage

statement: Reason 3 for soft delete - audit: deleted data may be needed as evidence later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The third one is audit.

statement: At a startup, one user harassed another online with a filthy comment; the victim filed a police complaint and police asked the platform for all details of the user. The harasser deleted the comment once they learned of the complaint - with a hard delete the evidence would be gone.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As soon as user A got to know that B has filed a complaint, A deleted it.

statement: As a consumer platform you have to provide such information to the authorities; police and government do not want evidence of harassment to disappear, which is why soft deletes are important.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because we are a consumer platform. We have to provide this information.

statement: The teacher personally visited a police station, gave justifications and handed over printed copies of all the traces - something an engineer would never expect to do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I visited police station giving justifications, printed copy of all the traces, handed it over to police, not even exaggerating a bit.

statement: When designing a table, ask whether its entries need recoverability, archival or audit; if yes, use soft delete, otherwise hard delete.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Would it require recoverability? Would it require archival? Would it require an audit? If yes, you do soft delete. Otherwise you do hard.

statement: Always design systems from a holistic view rather than a narrow view of just building things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you're designing system think from holistic view rather than just thinking from this very narrow vision of building things

statement: Another reason for soft deletes is that they are easy on the database: most storage engines store data as a B+ tree, and a hard delete removes the entry from a node, unbalancing the tree so it must be rebalanced, spending CPU cycles on rebalancing rather than on requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now when you hard delete a row, the entry gets deleted from the B plus tree node, B plus tree becomes imbalanced

statement: With a soft delete the entry is only updated (the column changes) and still exists, so the B+ tree node does not need rebalancing, which reduces load on the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So with soft deletes, your entry gets updated, your B plus tree node does not have to get rebalance because the entry still exists...

statement: Knowing database internals - how your database structures data - is really important to decide whether soft delete helps and to design the system accordingly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is why knowing the database internals is really important.

statement: In general, people soft delete in tables that store user-generated information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would always see this practice of people doing soft deletes in the database or in the tables that they store the user generated information.

statement: In the blog schema, bio (a user bio of about 140 characters) uses a short text type while body (a gigantic blog) uses a long text type; the database handles the storage difference internally.
detail: The bio was described as about 128 characters at 01:41:37 and about 140 characters here.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So body is a long text format. Bio is a short text format.

statement: In a row-based database all the data of a row is stored together in fixed-width rows, so the database knows exactly at which byte each column starts; every row needs a fixed length.
detail: Easiest to understand in relational databases, but also true for non-relational ones. Links back to the earlier example of an 8-byte entry made of two 4-byte fields.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in a row based database, base, you would see all the data of a particular row staying together. And these are fixed width rows.

statement: Fixed-width rows are exactly like C structs: you know the byte offset of each field.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's like exactly C structs that we know

statement: A varchar (short text) column is stored inline with the other columns of the row.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: With short text, when you define a text like this, it is a short text and it stays with the other columns of the row.

statement: A long text column is stored by the database in a separate location on disk (still disk, not network I/O), and the row keeps only a reference to it; the database does this internally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it stores this long text in a separate disk location.

statement: Reading a long text column costs two disk calls (one for the row, one for the text), making reads expensive; a short text column comes back with the row in one read, saving a disk call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you read it, it makes one DB, one disk call to read the row, another disk call to read this entire thing, right?
flags: asr: [?saves one disk call | asr: "says one disk column"]

statement: Long text is stored elsewhere because row length has to be limited: gigantic text cannot sit in rows, and small rows let the database scan rows easily.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have to limit the length of the row

statement: Email, bio, first name and last name are short text (varchar is what is typically used); a blog body or a long comment is long text.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So email is a short text. Bio is a short text. First name is a short text.

statement: If you allow 5,000-character comments, that is 5,000 bytes; storing it inline would make every row huge - a waste of space - so you must know when data is long enough to be stored separately.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say if you are allowing 5,000 characters comment, 5,000 characters is 5,000 bytes.

statement: Why not always store inline: listing pages read the blog title, first few lines/excerpt and image, not the body; the body is needed only when someone opens the blog page, so the extra disk read is paid only then.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But will you want to render the blog body every time when you're rendering it? No

statement: Always keep the row (or document) size to a bare minimum: store very large text as long text and everything else as short text.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: always try to keep the row size to a bare minimum.

statement: The published_at column stores when a blog was published; there are multiple ways to store a date time, each with different advantages - three approaches are discussed.
case_study: Multi-user blogging application like Medium: one user posts multiple blogs, many users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There are multiple ways to do that. And each one of them gives you different advantages.

statement: Approach 1: use the database's native date time column type, the most basic way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So every database provides you as a date time type of a particular column.

statement: A database storing a date time on disk serializes it in some format and flushes it; to read it, it reads that format from disk and converts it into a date time object before processing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if your database is storing data on the disk, it is serializing the data in some format and then flushing it.

statement: Hypothetical example: a date time like '2nd April 22090136Z' could naively be stored literally as a string on disk; every read then requires the engine to convert the string into a date time object for comparison.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: one naive way to do this is to store this date time literally as a string on the disk.
flags: check: example string "2nd April 22090136Z" as transcribed; board may show the exact format

statement: For a query like SELECT * FROM blogs WHERE published_at > now minus seven days, a database storing dates as strings must read the string of every row, extract date, month, year, hour, minute and second, and apply comparison logic (e.g. in its C++ code).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: select star from blogs where published at is greater than now minus seven days.

statement: Reading a date string from disk, converting it to a date time object and comparing is expensive; how your database stores this data on disk determines its performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: depending on how your database stores this data on the disk, it determines the performance of your database.

statement: Not all databases store date time as a string: MySQL, Postgres and MongoDB each have their own format; some store epoch seconds, some epoch milliseconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MySQL has its own format. Postgres has its own format. MongoDB has its own format.

statement: Understand how your database stores date time on disk; if it is not performant enough for your use case, don't use it and find another, more efficient way to store the information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So whichever database you are using, understand how it stores the date time on the disk.

statement: Storing dates as the native date type is extremely convenient (the language gives you a native date object for comparison) but may be suboptimal in some cases and can ruin performance.
detail: The teacher promises a practical example where this actually happened and a company moved away from it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It makes our life very easy, but it may be suboptimal in some cases.
flags: asr: [?storing date as a date | asr: "storing data as a data"]

statement: Approach 2: store date time as an epoch integer - a published_at column of integer type (not date time) holding the epoch; a lot of companies have started following this.
detail: Repeated at 02:00:04: a lot of people store date time as epoch integers in integer columns because they get a lot of benefits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you create a column published at whose type is integer and not date time and you store epoch in that.

statement: An epoch integer (epoch timestamp) is the number of seconds or milliseconds elapsed since 1 January 1970, 'where the clock started ticking'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: number of seconds or number of milliseconds elapsed since first January 1970.

statement: If a database stored the date time as that string, it would take about 20 bytes; the same information as an epoch integer takes 4 bytes - a massive space gain.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: From 20 bytes to four bytes, massive space gain, right?

statement: An epoch integer is efficient, optimal and lightweight but not readable: looking at the number you cannot tell what time it is, while a date time is readable at a glance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is efficient, optimal, lightweight, but not at all readable.

statement: Epoch integers are lightweight on the index: comparison is a plain integer comparison, the most efficient operation for the database, disk and computer in general, while a date time needs a complex multi-attribute object before comparing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It is very lightweight on index. It's just integer comparison.

statement: In 2016 Redbus (a bus-booking company) had a table storing date time as date time, and it became the performance bottleneck because of massive date time comparisons, slowing things down to the core.
detail: The teacher knows this example because one of his friends did it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In 2016, Redbus is where people do bus booking. They were having a table which stored date time as date time.

statement: Redbus considered epoch integers but would lose readability: their engineers rendered the value as-is in their SQL IDEs and UI and were used to debugging that way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If they moved to an epoch integer, they lost readability.

statement: Approach 3 (custom format): relax a constraint you don't need - Redbus needed only date granularity, not time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So they relax the constraint. They said, hey, we don't need time. What we need is we need date.

statement: Redbus stored the date as an integer in YYYYMMDD format (not a string), e.g. 20220402 for 2 April 2022 - a custom format heavily optimized for their use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So YYYYMMDD as an integer, not as a string, as an integer. So 20220402.

statement: The YYYYMMDD integer gives readability (you can see it is 2 April) and performance (integer comparison, integer index, lightning fast).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They get benefit because they get performance because it is integer. Integer comparison, integer index, lightning fast.

statement: There is no hard rule to use the date time type or epoch integers: be creative and open to altering constraints - that is where the next level of optimizations comes from.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Be creative with your solution. And that's where the next level of optimizations come.

statement: Each date time approach (native date time, epoch integer, custom integer format) has its own advantages and disadvantages; pick the type by asking whether you need readability, performance or convenience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Do you need readability? Do you need performance? Do you need convenience?

statement: A student objected that the YYYYMMDD custom format is inflexible if time is needed in the future; the answer: Redbus knew they did not need time.
detail: Question from a student (Student 3). The teacher: 'They knew they did not.'
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: because what I think is, this is really inflexible.

statement: A student argued Redbus could have stored epoch and parsed it on the client with a simple function, since the custom integer gives no performance improvement over epoch; the teacher agreed it is the same integer benefit, but they wanted readability and it was their decision.
detail: Teacher: 'They wanted readability.' / 'It's their decision, their company.' / 'Correct, that's all.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: They could have, they could have also stored as an epoch.
flags: check: segment at 02:04:00 may mix Teacher and Student 3 - "that's what I'm saying" sounds like Student 3

statement: The teacher has seen a bunch of places use custom date formats instead of native date time or epoch (details proprietary).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've seen a bunch of places where people have used custom format, I cannot reveal it because it's proprietary information

statement: A student pointed out that the native date time format can capture time zone information, which is somewhat lost in the epoch and custom formats, and must be considered when choosing a scheme.
detail: From a student (Student 8). The teacher: 'You get something, you lose something.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think with the first format, you also capture the time zone information, which is a little bit lost in second and third one.

statement: If time is stored in Unix (epoch) format, for viewing purposes you can render it in the local device's time zone wherever it is displayed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: depending on where the time is rendered, you can pick the local device system and render it in that.

statement: The same epoch value represents different local times in different time zones, so you must be especially careful to take everything in UTC (a student who had 'burned their hands' with this).
detail: From a student (Student 8); the teacher appears to agree ('everyone has been through this').
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: you need to be especially careful, like that you take everything in UTC.
flags: check: crosstalk - "yes, yes, yes" / "everyone has been" may be the Teacher

statement: No date time format is better than the others overall; each has its own trade-offs, and you choose the one that gives what you need.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not that, it's not that this is better than the both, right?

statement: The Redbus case was a production use case (not disclosed), more analytics than transactional, where date time comparisons were creating havoc and became the bottleneck, so they went with the custom format.
detail: Question from a student: why did Redbus not use epoch - was it only for development?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It was more of analytics use case, not for transactional systems, but date time was creating the havoc.
flags: asr: [?an epoch integer | asr: "a pocket teacher"]

statement: A student argued that the rebalancing benefit of soft deletes holds only if rows stay soft-deleted forever; when data is eventually hard deleted (e.g. Google Drive after 30 days), the database has to rebalance anyway.
detail: The teacher said 'No, no, no': hard deleting each row individually can, worst case, trigger a rebalance per delete, while accumulated soft deletes can be hard deleted in one batch so the tree is rebalanced once or a few times.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So it's beneficial only if you are in that soft delete state forever.

statement: Accumulating soft deletes and hard deleting them in one shot clubs the tree rebalancing together: the database rebalances once or a few times instead of (worst case) on every pointed delete.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what you are saving on is you are clubbing all the tree rebalancing into one

statement: Doing staggered, batched deletion - e.g. deleting 100 rows at a time and committing - gives one rebalance per 100 rows, slashing the number of rebalances by a factor of 100.
detail: Follows a student's remark that, for Google Drive, you could batch a day's hard deletes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you are slashing the number of rebalances by a factor of 100 by batching it in the size of 100.

statement: A student worried that the epoch number keeps increasing and will soon max out a 4-byte int, forcing a move to 64 bits, making epoch the worst format; the teacher agreed the point is very true.
detail: From a student (Sandeep), who had ranked epoch as the worst format.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: very soon you're going to max out on int, then you have to go to double, that will be like 64 bit.

statement: An epoch integer is 4 bytes today, and the integer range maxes out as soon as we hit 2032 (as stated); moving from 4 to 8 bytes doubles the space needed to store a date.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As soon as we hit 2032 is when we would limit, where we would basically max out, right?

statement: Because epoch starts at 1 January 1970, representing a date before it (e.g. 31 December 1969) requires negative numbers like -1, which the teacher calls wrong on so many levels.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if I do it with an epoch integer, I would have to represent it with minus one.

statement: An alternative is a compressed serialized date time that covers the entire date range without being limited by integer size, at a little extra space - about 6 bytes rather than 8 - as MySQL does.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say eight bytes, not eight bytes, but rather six bytes, but it can store it in a very compressed way.

statement: MySQL stores date time in a mind-blowingly efficient way, covering a massive range (from BCE up to, the teacher thinks, about 20,000 years) with very few bytes.
detail: Hedged by the teacher ('I think').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I think it supports still 20,000 year.

statement: Read MySQL's official datetime documentation, not a blog, video or random person: it explains why MySQL serializes date time instead of storing integers while still getting good enough performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read the official document. Don't read some blog or video or random person.

statement: MySQL's date time storage tries to balance both worlds: it is a serialized (non-integer) format that still gives good enough performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it tries to balance both worlds.
